title: Pantone
text: Pantone’s PMS system itself is proprietary and trademarked, so this mode doesn’t touch it. What it does cover is the Color of the Year – one color (twice, two) that the Pantone Color Institute names each December, publicly, in its own press releases. Pick a year below and copy the hex.

title: Wada
text:
Sanzo Wada was a Japanese textile and costume designer whose 1933 reference book, A Dictionary of Color Combinations (配色総鑑), catalogued 348 named colors alongside hundreds of pre-tested pairings meant to be visually harmonious together – closer to a curated palette-pairing tool than a raw color list. Each base color in this mode’s data is matched to one, two, or three other colors Wada specifically paired with it, giving combos of 2, 3, or 4 total colors.
Palette Jack’s Wada mode lets you pick a combo size, randomize to one of Wada’s own matched sets, and copy it straight into scale_fill_manual().

title: Wada
text:
Source

Wada, S. (1933). Haishoku Sōkan [配色総鑑 / A Dictionary of Color Combinations]. Kyoto: Kōrinsha. Reissued: Wada, S. (2019). A Dictionary of Color Combinations. Seigensha Art Publishing. ISBN 978-4-86152-568-1.

title: Werner
text:
Abraham Gottlob Werner was a German geologist who, in the late 1700s, developed a standardized color-naming system so mineralogists could describe rock and mineral color consistently. In 1814 (2nd ed. 1821), Scottish flower painter Patrick Syme illustrated and expanded Werner’s system into 110 named colors, organized into 10 classifications (White, Grey, Black, Blue, Purple, Green, Yellow, Orange, Red, Brown) – each cross-referenced against an animal, a plant, and a mineral where that color occurs in nature. Charles Darwin carried a copy on the Beagle to describe organisms and landscapes with a shared, precise color vocabulary.
Palette Jack’s Werner mode lets you filter by classification and pull a randomized set of these historical colors as a ready-to-paste hex list – useful for quick categorical palettes, or just for the pleasure of finding out your data happens to be “Arterial Blood Red” or “Skimmed-milk White.”

title: Werner
section: How many colors should you randomize?
text:
How many colors should you randomize?
There’s no universal “right” number, but two lines of vision-science research give a useful working range:

Below ~4, people reliably hold and recall a set of colors in visual working memory – the classic estimate from change-detection tasks (Luck & Vogel, 1997; Ngiam et al., 2023).
Beyond roughly 8-10, categorical color palettes get measurably harder to read accurately, and common design tools (e.g. ColorBrewer’s qualitative sets) cap out around 12 (Healey, 1996; Tseng et al., 2023).

So the randomizer below defaults to 5 colors and caps at 12 – past that point you’re better served by a sequential or continuous scale than a hand-picked categorical one.

Sources & citations

Werner, A. G. (1814). Werner’s Nomenclature of Colours (P. Syme, Ed. & Ill., 2nd ed., 1821). Edinburgh: William Blackwood.


Luck, S. J., & Vogel, E. K. (1997). The capacity of visual working memory for features and conjunctions. Nature, 390(6657), 279-281. https://doi.org/10.1038/36846


Ngiam, W. X. Q., Loetscher, K. B., & Awh, E. (2023). Object-based encoding constrains storage in visual working memory. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 153(1), 86-101. https://doi.org/10.1037/xge0001479


Healey, C. G. (1996). Choosing effective colours for data visualization. Proceedings of the 7th IEEE Conference on Visualization, 263-270. https://doi.org/10.1109/visual.1996.568118


Tseng, C., Bearfield, C. X., & Franconeri, S. (2023). Measuring categorical perception in color-coded scatterplots. Proceedings of the 2023 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems. https://doi.org/10.1145/3544548.3581416

title: Wada
Woods Hole
text:
The palettes

Show the code
library(tidyverse)
library(glue)

woods_hole <- read_csv("../data/woods-hole-palettes.csv")

swatch_html <- function(hex, cap = 8) {
  n <- length(hex)
  shown <- head(hex, cap)
  spans <- glue('<span class="mini-swatch" style="background:{shown}"></span>')
  out <- paste(spans, collapse = "")
  if (n > cap) out <- paste0(out, glue('<span class="palette-module-more">+{n - cap} more</span>'))
  out
}

gallery <- woods_hole |>
  arrange(palette, position) |>
  group_by(palette, display_name, description) |>
  summarise(
    n_colors = n(),
    swatches = swatch_html(hex),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(display_name)

cat(
  '<div class="palette-gallery">',
  glue_data(
    gallery,
    '<div class="palette-module">
  <h4>{display_name} <span class="palette-module-count">{n_colors} colors</span></h4>
  <p class="palette-module-desc">{description}</p>
  <div class="palette-module-swatches">{swatches}</div>
</div>'
  ),
  '</div>',
  sep = "\n"
)
